title: Ahijah's Word to Jeroboam and Shishak's Raid on Jerusalem
summary: When Jeroboam's son Abijah falls ill, Jeroboam sends his wife in disguise to the blind prophet Ahijah, who sees through the disguise and announces the destruction of Jeroboam's house and the future exile of Israel; the boy dies as she returns home. In Judah, Rehoboam's reign is marked by idolatry, and Shishak of Egypt plunders the temple and palace, carrying off Solomon's gold shields, which Rehoboam replaces with bronze.
story: The prophet who once handed Jeroboam ten pieces of a torn cloak (11:29-39) now reverses the blessing, because Jeroboam refused its condition. The chapter then turns south and shows that Judah is no better: the kingdom that kept the temple fills the land with high places and Asherah poles. From here Kings alternates between the two kingdoms, moving back and forth reign by reign, and each account is closed with a regular formula. Ahijah's words in verses 15-16 look far down the road to the Assyrian exile of the north, and the bronze shields of verse 27 quietly measure how far Solomon's splendor has fallen in a few years.
historical:
Shishak's campaign (verse 25) is one of the best-attested events of the period outside the Bible. Sheshonq I of Egypt (reigned about 945 to 924 BC) recorded a military campaign into Canaan on a relief at the temple of Amun at Karnak, listing many place names, mostly in the Negev and in the northern kingdom; a fragment of a victory monument bearing his name was also found at Megiddo. The list is damaged, and Jerusalem does not clearly appear in what survives, which fits the Bible's account that Jerusalem paid rather than fell. The fifth year of Rehoboam is usually dated about 926 or 925 BC.

Tirzah (verse 17), in the hills northeast of Shechem, served as a royal residence and later as the northern capital until Omri moved it to Samaria. The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel and of Judah (verses 19 and 29) were royal records the writer of Kings used and cited; they are lost and are not the biblical books of Chronicles. Rehoboam's mother, Naamah, is twice called an Ammonite (verses 21 and 31), a reminder of Solomon's foreign marriages in chapter 11.
cultural:
Consulting a prophet about a sick child was normal, and a gift of food (verse 3) was the expected payment. Jeroboam sends his wife in disguise because he knows he has broken with the prophet who made him king and fears an unwelcome answer. The curse of verse 11, with bodies eaten by dogs and birds, describes the worst fate an ancient person could imagine: to lie unburied, cut off from family and honor. That is why verse 13 counts it a mercy that the child will be mourned and buried.

The sacred pillars and Asherah poles of verse 23 were fixtures of Canaanite worship. Asherah was a goddess known from texts at Ugarit and elsewhere, and the Asherah was a wooden pole or stylized tree that represented her at shrines. Inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud and Khirbet el-Qom in the eighth century BC, which mention the LORD and his asherah, show that some Israelites combined her worship with the LORD's, precisely what the prophets condemned. The male shrine prostitutes of verse 24 translate a Hebrew term (qadesh) meaning a consecrated person; whether it refers to ritual prostitution or to other cultic roles is debated among scholars.
literary: The chapter has two parts joined by the theme of losing what God gave. Verses 1-18 are a prophetic scene built on irony: a blind prophet sees through a disguise the king's wife thinks will deceive him, and the one who came to learn her son's future learns the future of her whole house. Ahijah's speech follows the standard shape of prophetic judgment, reminding Jeroboam of God's gifts (verses 7-8), naming his sin (verse 9), and announcing the penalty (verses 10-16). The narrator then confirms fulfillment in verse 18. Verses 19-31 switch into the book's regular regnal formulas, the pattern of accession, evaluation, events, sources, death, and successor that will frame every reign that follows.

outline.t: Jeroboam's wife goes in disguise to Ahijah
Ahijah's judgment on the house of Jeroboam and on Israel
The child dies; the end of Jeroboam's reign
Shishak takes the gold; bronze shields replace it

doctrines.note: Ahijah announces judgment on Jeroboam's house and, further off, on Israel as a nation. Both are rooted in specific sins: images made to provoke the LORD and a people led into sin by their king.
The north has its calves; the south has its high places, pillars, and Asherah poles. Neither kingdom is free of idolatry, and the chapter refuses to let Judah feel superior because it has the temple.
Even in judgment God notices good. The one child in Jeroboam's house in whom the LORD found something good is spared the dishonor coming on the rest and is mourned by all Israel.

words.note: Ka'as, to provoke to anger or vex. It becomes a refrain in Kings for idolatry (verses 9 and 15). The word pictures God not as coldly offended but as personally grieved and angered by a people who turn to other gods.

Qana, to be jealous or zealous. Judah provoked the LORD to jealous anger (verse 22). In the Bible God's jealousy is the protective passion of a husband for his covenant partner, not petty envy; it assumes a relationship that idolatry betrays.

Asherah, the name of a Canaanite goddess and of the wooden cult object that represented her. Its appearance in both halves of the chapter (verses 15 and 23) links the northern and southern kingdoms in the same sin.

christ: Ahijah's prophecy that Israel would be uprooted and scattered beyond the Euphrates came true when Assyria conquered the north in 722 BC. The prophets later promised that God would gather his scattered people again (Jeremiah 31; Ezekiel 37), and the New Testament presents Jesus as the shepherd who gathers the lost sheep of Israel and then the nations (John 10:16). The chapter also sets a pattern that deepens the need for a better king: the first northern king and the first king of the divided Judah both failed, and the gold of Solomon's glory was carried off to Egypt within five years of his death. The longing for a son of David whose glory could not be taken away is a thematic thread here, not a prediction within the chapter.

hard.q: Why does the one good child in Jeroboam's house die?
hard.a: The text frames the boy's death as a strange mercy within judgment. Ahijah says he alone will be buried and mourned by all Israel because the LORD found something good in him (verse 13). The rest of Jeroboam's house will die violently and lie unburied when Baasha seizes the throne (15:29). In the ancient view, a peaceful death and an honored burial were far better than what was coming. Many readers still find this difficult, and the chapter does not claim to answer every question about the suffering of the innocent. It does insist that God saw the child, valued him, and did not treat him as merely part of his father's guilt. Isaiah 57:1-2 expresses a similar thought: the righteous are sometimes taken away from evil to come.

questions: Jeroboam's wife went in disguise, but the prophet saw through it at once. In what ways do people try to approach God while hiding who they are?
Rehoboam replaced gold shields with bronze and kept up the ceremony. Where might people keep the outward form of something after its substance is gone?
The LORD found something good in one child in a corrupt household. What does that suggest about how God sees individuals within families and institutions?
